newsitem.title: UK: Elf diverts crude as refinery strike bites - trade.
newsitem.headline: Elf diverts crude as refinery strike bites - trade.

text.p: French oil company Elf Aquitaine has been forced to divert or sell millions of barrels of crude oil as a result of a crippling strike at three of its refineries but so far the sales have created few waves in the spot market, traders said.

Oil traders said Elf, which has been hit by an eight-day-old strike shutting in nearly a quarter of the country's refining capacity, was offering a mid-December 500,000-barrel cargo of Norwegian Gullfaks crude.
"I think they've done a few things apart from that," said a trader for a major North Sea oil producer.
Elf said it did not comment on trading transactions.
The company produces about 270,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil from the North Sea, which is split between its own refining system and spot market sales.
Traders said more cargoes could be offered for sale if talks between the company and unions on Thursday fail to end the strike over pay and working conditions.
The strike could escalate next week with unions calling for an industry-wide, one-day stoppage throughout France on Tuesday.

The Elf plants affected are the 98,000 bpd Grandpuits refinery near Paris, fed with crude from the port of Le Havre, the 214,000 bpd Donges refinery in western France supplied via Nantes, and the 128,000 bpd Feyzin refinery near Lyon which takes crude by pipeline from the Mediterranean port of Fos.
A Mediterranean crude trader said Elf was offering cargoes but did not appear to be in any rush to sell.
"They are offering a range of things but not at distressed prices."

In northwest Europe, traders said Elf was not looking to buy crude on the spot market and was selling or diverting equity crude to other French refiners producing flat out to make up for the shortfall in inland product supply.
"Those guys are laughing all the way to the bank at the moment," said one.
"Elf's definitely not there to buy anything at the moment, they'll be delaying and balancing their supply arrangements," said another trader.
Another option for Elf would be to divert crude to Britain, where its has a 70 percent share in the 120,000 bpd Milford Haven refinery.
Traders said Elf would want to keep crude stocks relatively high in the event of the strike being called off at short notice.
"If they run out of both crude and (refined) products that would be a very dangerous situation," said a trader.
Reduced demand from Elf was having no noticeable impact on the spot market for North Sea crude, with remaining December supply thin.
Sellers were also reporting strong interest in North Sea crude, particularly benchmark Brent, from the United States.
